title: Articles and generic reference
objectives: Distinguish general and specific noun reference.
Use articles with singular countable nouns.
Recognise countable uses of normally uncountable nouns.

explanation.heading: Meaning and use
paragraphs: Generic reference means talking about a class or substance in general rather than a particular example. ‘Dogs need exercise’ makes a general statement about dogs. ‘Water is essential’ refers to water generally. In these sentences, plural countable nouns and uncountable nouns commonly appear without an article.

The can identify a specific group or amount: ‘The dogs next door are barking’ and ‘The water in this bottle is warm’. The context and any identifying phrase help the listener understand which dogs or water are intended. An article choice can therefore change the reference, not merely the grammar.

explanation.heading: Form
paragraphs: A singular countable noun normally requires a determiner. ‘A dog needs exercise’ can make a general statement about a representative member of a class. ‘The tiger is a large cat’ can refer to the species as a whole in a suitable context, especially in factual writing. These forms are not interchangeable in every sentence; the intended meaning and noun matter.

Use a or an for one non-specific singular countable item: ‘I need a pen’. Use the when the item is identifiable in context: ‘Please pass me the pen on the desk’. An is chosen before a vowel sound and a before a consonant sound: an hour but a university.

explanation.heading: Examples in context
paragraphs: Compare ‘Books can be expensive’ with ‘The books on the shelf are expensive’. The first concerns books generally; the second concerns a particular set. Compare ‘Coffee contains caffeine’ with ‘The coffee in my cup is cold’. Coffee can also be countable when referring to servings: ‘Two coffees, please’.

Some common phrases have established article patterns: ‘play the piano’ is common in British English, while ‘play piano’ is also used, especially in American English and in some contexts. Institutional phrases such as ‘go to school’ and ‘go to the school’ can differ in meaning and depend on context; they require more than a simple general-versus-specific rule.

explanation.heading: Contrasts and common mistakes
paragraphs: Do not put a or an directly before an uncountable noun in its ordinary uncountable meaning: say ‘some information’ or ‘a piece of information’, not ‘an information’. Do not assume the is always incorrect before a plural or uncountable noun: ‘the information in this report’ identifies a specific set of information.

A sentence with a plural noun and no article is not automatically a universal law. ‘Dogs can be friendly’ is a generalisation, not a claim that every dog is friendly. Article use involves reference, meaning and context; in controlled questions, the intended general or specific reference is stated explicitly.

summary: Bare plural and uncountable nouns often express generic reference.
The can identify a particular group or amount; singular generic forms are also possible in suitable contexts.
Article choice depends on meaning, context and established patterns.

exercises.prompt: Make a general statement about dogs: ___ need exercise.
exercises.explanation: The bare plural expresses the intended general reference.

option_feedback.b: “Dogs” fits here. The bare plural expresses the intended general reference.
option_feedback.c: “A dogs” does not fit here. The bare plural expresses the intended general reference.
option_feedback.d: “The dogs in this room” does not fit here. The bare plural expresses the intended general reference.
